back: One dot per value above a number line; equal values stack up. Good for small numerical data sets.
Shows the five-number summary: whiskers to the minimum and maximum, a box from $Q_1$ to $Q_3$, and a line at the median.

front: What fraction of the data is in each section of a box plot?
back: About a quarter (25%), whatever the length of the section.
Bars for numerical data grouped into equal class intervals. The bars touch and the heights are frequencies.
Bar graph: categories, with gaps between bars. Histogram: a numerical scale in intervals, bars touching.
Shows the relationship between two numerical variables; each point is one person or thing.
The variable that might explain or influence the other. It goes on the x-axis.
The variable that may respond to (depend on) the other. It goes on the y-axis.
A line drawn by eye through the middle of the points, following the trend, used to make predictions.
Shows one variable over time: time on the x-axis, points joined by lines. Look for a trend and repeating patterns.
A table showing counts for two categorical variables at once, with row and column totals.
How the values of a numerical variable are spread out: where they cluster, how spread out they are, and any unusual values.
